claim: Ring all-reduce's normalized per-worker communication load is 2(N-1)/N, i.e. independent of worker count for large N.
stance_target: baseline cost model for DDP gradient all-reduce
quoted_support: For a system with N workers, its normalized per-worker communication is 2(N −1)/N.

claim: CERAR's coded approximate ring all-reduce achieves normalized per-worker communication 1+(N-2)/c over L=c+N-2 rounds, strictly below ring's 2(N-1)/N whenever c>N.
stance_target: coded/approximate all-reduce can cut DDP payload below the ring lower bound
scope_conditions: N workers, c gradient chunks, bounded approximation error
quoted_support: CERAR partitions each local gradient into c components and crucially relies on linear encoding and decoding operations. It performs L = c + N −2 communication rounds over an N-worker ring, yielding normalized communication rate 1+(N −2)/c and normalized storage rate 1+N/c.

claim: On an 8-GPU A100 PCIe node (31.5 GB/s interconnect), CERAR cuts raw all-reduce time by 46.0-47.1% versus production NCCL.
stance_target: approximate all-reduce is a large lever on a PCIe-limited fabric
scope_conditions: single node, 8x A100 PCIe, FP32 tensors, 31.5 GB/s interconnect
quoted_support: As shown in Table I, CERAR outperforms the NCCL implementation on the A100 PCIe system, reducing the reduction time by 46.0–47.1%. However, on the H200 NVLink system, CERAR is 33.2%–33.9% slower than NCCL.

claim: The absolute all-reduce win on PCIe is large in wall-clock terms: a 1B-entry FP32 tensor drops from 17,954.4 ms under NCCL to 9,558.6 ms under CERAR (46.8%).
stance_target: coded all-reduce reduces absolute collective latency at LLM-scale gradient sizes
scope_conditions: 8x A100 PCIe, 1B FP32 entries per GPU, c=20, L=26

claim: End-to-end, Pythia-1.4B training on 4x A100 PCIe 40GB drops from 3.79 h (NCCL) to 3.14 h (CERAR), a 17.3% reduction, with essentially identical validation loss (1.4218 vs 1.4213).
stance_target: approximate gradient aggregation does not degrade training quality at 1.4B scale
scope_conditions: Pythia-1.4B, TinyStories, 4x A100 PCIe 40GB, 1800 steps (~117.96M tokens), c=12, L=14
quoted_support: As shown in Table II, on the PCIe configuration, NCCL requires 3.79 hours, whereas CERAR requires 3.14 hours; the corresponding validation losses at the end of the 1800 iterations are 1.4218 and 1.4213 respectively.

claim: Throughput on that PCIe run rises from 8,644 to 10,451 tokens/s at a cost of +2.4 GB peak memory (36.2 -> 38.6 GB).
stance_target: coded all-reduce buys throughput at modest memory cost
quoted_support: 4× A100 PCIe 40GB (PCIe interconnect): 1,800 steps ... NCCL All-Reduce 3.79 8,644 1.4218 36.2 ... Our algorithm 3.14 10,451 1.4213 38.6

claim: On a high-bandwidth NVLink fabric the same scheme is a net loss: 3.65% slower end-to-end (4.745 h vs 4.578 h) on 4x A100 SXM 80GB.
stance_target: coded approximate all-reduce is universally beneficial
scope_conditions: 4x A100 SXM 80GB, NVLink, Pythia-1.4B, 7630 steps (~1e9 tokens)
quoted_support: On the SXM configuration, NCCL and our algorithm require 4.578 and 4.745 hours, respectively. The validation losses of both schemes are approximately 1.16449. However, our algorithm takes 3.65% longer.

claim: The approximation error is real but argued benign: relative l2 gradient error of ~1.61%, 2.87% and 2.72% at steps 1, 3815 and 7630, versus <7e-9 for NCCL.
quoted_support: For our algorithm, these errors are approximately 1.61%, 2.87%, and 2.72%, respectively, while those for NCCL are below 7 × 10−9 (consistent with floating-point roundoff). Nevertheless, these errors do not impact the training in an appreciable manner.

claim: The premise that makes the scheme usable is that approximate gradient recovery suffices for SGD-style training.
stance_target: lossy/approximate gradient aggregation is safe for LLM pretraining
quoted_support: We note that approximate recovery often suffices in scenarios such as distributed parameter training, i.e., instead of true gradients, we often settle for approximate gradients which do not affect the quality of training much.

claim: CERAR's advantage is bandwidth-regime dependent by construction: it wins on low-bandwidth PCIe and loses on high-bandwidth NVLink.
stance_target: the value of communication compression scales inversely with fabric bandwidth
quoted_support: On the other hand, for GPU clusters with high-bandwidth NVLink interconnects, CERAR performs worse on the All-Reduce phase time and slightly worse in terms of training.

claim: The reported gains are a lower bound: the authors describe their implementation as an unoptimised proof of concept relative to NCCL.
quoted_support: Our implementation of CERAR is meant more as a proof of concept and the implementation has not been optimized anywhere close to the level of NCCL.

claim: The measured all-reduce times include encoding, all communication rounds with local updates, and decoding, so the arithmetic overhead is already inside the reported numbers.
stance_target: whether encoding/decoding cost is excluded from CERAR's reported gains
scope_conditions: A100 PCIe and H200 SXM experiments
quoted_support: For our algorithm, this includes (i) encoding (preparing δi,j’s), (ii) all communication rounds and their local updates, and (iii) decoding using the stored values and the Ri matrices to reconstruct the approximate sum.

claim: The asymptotically exact Vandermonde construction is numerically ill-conditioned; the authors give an alternate construction with error O(eps) and condition number O(eps^-r*), r*=ceil(c/N)-1.
scope_conditions: linear encoding/decoding matrices over an N-worker ring
quoted_support: Accordingly, we give an alternate construction whose error is O(ϵ), while the relevant condition numbers are O(ϵ−r⋆), where r⋆= ⌈c/N⌉−1.

claim: CERAR is orthogonal to gradient quantisation and sparsification and can be stacked with them.
quoted_support: These approaches address communication reduction along a direction orthogonal to ours. Specifically, it may be possible to apply our techniques in conjunction with them.

claim: Transferability caveat: the tested 'low-bandwidth' PCIe fabric is 31.5 GB/s, roughly 30x the ~0.75 GiB/s NCCL all-reduce measured on the CMP 170HX box, so the direction of the effect should hold but the magnitude is not transferable.
stance_target: applicability of CERAR's measured gains to a PCIe Gen2 x4 CMP 170HX box
scope_conditions: single-node A100 PCIe vs 5x CMP 170HX Gen2 x4
quoted_support: We considered GPU clusters under two different settings - a low-bandwidth (PCIe, 31.5 GB/s) and a high-bandwidth (NVLink, ≥300 GB/s) interconnect.

claim: The scheme's parameters are tuned per fabric: c=20/L=26 on A100 PCIe, c=12/L=14 on H200 NVLink.
scope_conditions: A100 PCIe and H200 SXM experiments
quoted_support: CERAR used c = 20, L = 26 for the A100 experiments and c = 12, L = 14 for the H200 experiments.
